note: Non-temporal polity: institutional descriptions, political theory, rights concepts, peace/conflict theory, international-org types. Awaiting future non-temporal polity architecture. NOT mistags — these are legitimate polity content that doesn not fit the timeline.

nodes.label: Parliamentary System
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: System where executive is responsible to legislature. PM and Council of Ministers must retain confidence of Lok Sabha. Adopted from British model. Key reason: familiarity and accountability — India had experience with this system under colonial rule.

nodes.label: Fundamental Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12-35). Six categories of justiciable rights enforceable by courts. Can be amended but basic structure cannot be destroyed. Different from ordinary legal rights — protected by Constitution itself.

nodes.label: Right Against Exploitation
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking, begar (forced labour). Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous occupations.

nodes.label: Right to Freedom of Religion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Freedom of conscience, profession, practice and propagation of religion (Art 25). Right to manage religious affairs (Art 26). No tax for religious promotion (Art 27). No religious instruction in state-funded institutions (Art 28).

nodes.label: Cultural and Educational Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Article 29: Protection of interests of minorities (language, script, culture). Article 30: Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions. State cannot discriminate in granting aid.

nodes.label: Cultural Relativism vs Universal Rights
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Debate between universality of human rights and cultural specificity. Universalists: some rights apply everywhere. Relativists: rights are culturally defined. NCERT argues for minimum universal standards while respecting cultural diversity.

nodes.label: Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: More than absence of war: includes absence of structural violence, presence of justice, and conditions for human flourishing. Positive peace requires social justice, equality, and respect for rights. Central to NCERT political theory curriculum.

nodes.label: Negative Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Mere absence of direct violence or war. Does not address underlying causes like inequality, oppression, or exploitation. A ceasefire without addressing root causes is negative peace. Fragile and temporary without structural change.

nodes.label: Positive Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Presence of social justice, equality, and conditions for human development. Requires addressing structural violence (poverty, discrimination, exploitation). Johan Galtung's framework. Sustainable and durable peace built on justice.

nodes.label: Johan Galtung
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Norwegian peace researcher, founder of peace and conflict studies. Distinguished between positive and negative peace, and between direct and structural violence. His framework is foundational to understanding peace in political theory.

nodes.label: Just War Theory
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Theory that war can be morally justified under certain conditions: just cause, last resort, proportional means, legitimate authority, reasonable chance of success. Originated with Augustine and Aquinas. Critiqued by pacifists who reject all war.

nodes.label: Conflict Resolution
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Methods for resolving disputes without violence: negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dialogue. Requires addressing underlying causes and building trust. International institutions like UN provide mechanisms. Domestic courts provide legal resolution.

nodes.label: Nuclear Weapons and Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Nuclear weapons pose existential threat to humanity. Deterrence theory argues they prevent war; critics argue they make annihilation possible. NCERT discusses debates around nuclear disarmament and India's no-first-use policy.

nodes.label: Civil Disobedience
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Deliberate, public, non-violent breaking of unjust laws to bring about change. Differs from ordinary lawbreaking: done openly, accepts punishment, aims at justice. Thoreau, Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr. practiced it. Legitimate form of political protest.

nodes.label: United Nations and Peace
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: UN established in 1945 to maintain international peace and security. Security Council can authorize use of force. Peacekeeping operations, diplomatic mediation, international law. India is a major contributor to UN peacekeeping.

nodes.label: Boycott as Political Protest
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Form of political protest derived from the name of Captain Charles Boycott in Ireland (1880). UPSC 1996 tested: among boycott, gherao, bandh, and hartal, boycott is derived from a person's name. Non-violent method of protest through withdrawal of cooperation.

nodes.label: Hegemony as Structural Power
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: US shapes the global economy through Bretton Woods institutions (World Bank, IMF, WTO). Provides global public goods like sea-lanes of communication and the Internet. US economy is 28% of world GDP. The MBA degree is an example of structural hegemony.

nodes.label: UN Specialised Agencies
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Include WHO (health), UNDP (development), UNHRC (human rights), UNHCR (refugees), UNICEF (children), UNESCO (education, science, culture). Deal with social and economic issues alongside the General Assembly and Security Council.

nodes.label: Amnesty International
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: NGO campaigning for protection of human rights worldwide. Promotes respect for all rights in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Prepares reports on human rights that governments are often unhappy with.

nodes.label: Human Rights Watch
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Largest international human rights organisation in the US. Involved in research and advocacy. Draws media attention to abuses. Helped build campaigns to ban landmines, stop child soldiers, and establish the International Criminal Court.

nodes.label: Cooperative Security
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Non-traditional threats require cooperation rather than military confrontation. Can be bilateral, regional, or global. Involves international organisations (UN, WHO, World Bank), NGOs (Amnesty, Red Cross), businesses, and influential personalities. Force only as last resort, collectively sanctioned.

nodes.label: Women Suffrage Movement
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: The struggle by women to gain the right to vote. Suffragettes chained themselves to railings, were imprisoned, and went on hunger strikes. American women won voting rights in 1920; UK women achieved equal voting terms with men in 1928. World War I accelerated this movement.

nodes.label: Gandhi on Universal Franchise
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Gandhiji argued in Young India (1931) that every adult should have the right to vote. He could not accept that a man with wealth should vote while a man of character but without wealth or literacy should not. He demanded universal adult franchise before Independence.

nodes.label: Phases of Democracy Expansion
nodes.subject: polity
nodes.detail: Democracy expanded in phases: pre-1900 (W. Europe, N. America), 1900-1950 (Europe, Latin America), post-1945 decolonisation (Asia, Africa), post-1989 (Eastern Europe). By 2000, over half the world's countries were democracies.
